content: The guidelines on pesticide resistance management provide detailed instructions on how to minimize the development of resistance to pesticides in agricultural settings while ensuring effective crop protection. These guidelines are specifically designed for scientific, technical, and policy experts involved in creating or evaluating pesticide resistance management plans, as well as for regulators assessing the risk of resistance during the registration or renewal of pesticide products. They address the causes of resistance, outline objectives and challenges in managing it, and provide methods to assess the likelihood of resistance development. The guidelines also describe strategies and practices for preventing and managing resistance, methods for detecting and verifying resistance in the field, and examples of successful resistance prevention in transgenic Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) crops. Additionally, they include resources and internet links to real-world examples of resistance management plans. While the primary focus is on agriculture, the guidelines briefly touch on resistance in vectors of human diseases, with references to WHO guidelines for further information. New methods, such as the intensity bioassay and synergist bioassay, are introduced to measure the intensity of insecticide resistance and identify underlying metabolic mechanisms. Data from these tests enable countries to monitor the evolution of resistance, develop national resistance management strategies, and optimize the use of available tools. These procedures can also be adapted for testing resistance in mosquito vectors of other diseases. The guidelines on reporting systems for health and environmental incidents caused by pesticide exposure aim to assist governments in establishing basic reporting systems. They detail the type of information to collect, methods for collection, and criteria for determining whether risk mitigation or in-depth monitoring is required. They also explain how to investigate incidents, verify data quality, and define the roles of authorities responsible for collecting and utilizing the information. Sample questionnaires and reporting forms developed by WHO and the Rotterdam Convention Secretariat are provided, along with references for creating self-surveillance structures in resource-limited settings. The guidelines on post-registration surveillance outline activities to ensure pesticides are handled, distributed, and used safely and in compliance with approved labels and regulations. They cover monitoring pesticide use, quality, residues in food and the environment, and accidental poisoning. They also address training for farmers, retailers, extension workers, and medical practitioners, as well as licensing pesticide handlers and enforcing regulations on imports, advertisements, packaging, and labeling. The importance of information exchange among governments to stay updated on pesticide-related developments is emphasized. The International Code of Conduct on Pesticide Management, developed by FAO and WHO, provides a framework and standards for managing pesticides throughout their lifecycle. It is widely recognized as a reference for pesticide management and is directed at government authorities, the pesticide industry, and other stakeholders. The current version, published in 2014, places greater emphasis on public health pesticides, the health and environmental impacts of pesticides, and the management of highly hazardous pesticides. It also updates terms and definitions and aligns guidance with developments in industrial chemical management. The Code includes articles addressing objectives, terms, pesticide management, testing, risk reduction, regulatory requirements, availability, distribution, information exchange, labeling, advertising, and disposal.
